text:
For the reply you keep putting off, tap the microphone and talk through your answer, ums and all. Then paste the email and your ramble into ChatGPT or Claude:

Turn my notes into a reply to this email. Keep my wording where it works, cut the rest, under 120 words. Email: [paste] My notes: [paste]

It sounds like you because most of it is you. Shortcut 2 in my free guide is built for fast replies, linked in my profile.

Gmail has search codes that can find almost any email, and AI can write them for you. Describe what you're after:

Write a Gmail search that finds [emails from the school with attachments from the last 3 months]. Explain each part in a few words.

Paste it into the search bar, then click Create filter so those emails get a label automatically from now on. Which email do you always struggle to find?

Paste three things you've written into ChatGPT or Claude and ask:

Describe my writing style as 6 specific rules, with an example of each from my samples.

Save those rules in the app's custom instructions or in a project, and every draft starts out sounding like you. Prompt 11, Teach it your voice, goes further, and it's in my $7 shortcuts pack in my profile.

Upload screenshots of three months of bank or card statements, with the account numbers covered, and ask:

Find every recurring charge, including yearly ones. Flag any that went up in price across these months and give me the total yearly cost.

Small price increases are easy to miss one month at a time. Shortcut 9 in my free guide spots subscriptions to cancel, linked in my profile.

Before you put money into a new idea, like a side business or a course, ask the AI to find the weak spots:

Here's my idea: [describe]. Give me the 5 most likely reasons it fails, ranked, and a cheap test for each that I could run this month.

Run the cheapest test first. Prompt 36, Find the holes in my idea, is in my $7 shortcuts pack in my profile.

Before a hard conversation with a landlord or a manager, rehearse it out loud. Open voice mode in ChatGPT and say:

Play [person]. I'm going to ask for [what I want]. Push back the way they realistically would. After 5 back-and-forths, step out of character and tell me where I sounded unsure.

Run it twice and the real one feels familiar. Who would you most want to practice with?

When the school sends the year's dates as a PDF or a photo, ChatGPT or Claude can turn it into a calendar file you import in one go:

Turn every date in this into an .ics calendar file. Use [time zone], add a reminder the evening before each one, and list any dates you weren't sure about.

Check the unsure ones, then open the file on your phone. Which schedule would you hand off first?

Adding one line to the end of almost any request makes the answer fit your life much better:

Before you answer, ask me questions one at a time until you have what you need. Keep it to 5 questions at most.

It helps most with meal plans and trip plans, where the first answer usually comes out generic. What's a request you'd try this on first?

When the family group chat has eighty messages you missed, take a few screenshots of them, open ChatGPT, tap the plus button to add the pictures, and ask:

Summarize these messages in a few lines. List any plans, dates or questions that need an answer from me.

Screenshots work in any chat app. Shortcut 4 in my free guide, Summarize a long thread, is linked in my profile.

When an email asks you five different things, it's easy to answer three and miss two. Paste it into ChatGPT with this:

List every question this email asks me. Then write a short, friendly reply that answers each one using my notes. Email: [paste] My notes: [paste]

Your notes can be quick and messy. Shortcut 2 in my free guide, Reply to anything fast, is linked in my profile.

Turning someone down gets easier when you can choose how firm to be. Ask for the reply at two strengths:

Write a reply declining [request] from [person]. Give me a warm version that offers [alternative] and a firm version that says no kindly in two sentences.

Pick one, change a few words so it sounds like you, and send it. Shortcut 3 in my free guide, Say no without guilt, is linked in my profile.

On Monday morning, open ChatGPT, tap the microphone and talk through everything on your mind for the week. Then ask:

Turn what I said into a plan for this week with a first step for each item. Then tell me what I'm likely forgetting that usually comes with tasks like these.

That last line catches things like booking the dog sitter for a trip. Shortcut 6 in my free guide is linked in my profile.

If you use WhatsApp, you may already have an AI assistant without downloading anything. In many countries there's now a colorful ring icon on the Chats screen, and tapping it opens Meta AI. Try this first:

Give me 5 everyday ways you could help someone who runs a busy household, with one example question for each.

Then ask it one of its own examples. Have you spotted that ring on your phone yet?

The first answer an AI gives is only a starting point, and you can reply to it like a text. When an answer feels too technical, write back:

Say that again in simpler words, with one example from everyday life. Keep it under 100 words.

You can keep going until it makes sense, and it never gets impatient. What's a topic you'd like explained this way?

For the mystery cable in the drawer or the part that snapped off the dishwasher, open ChatGPT, tap the plus button, take a photo and ask:

What is this, what is it usually called, and what should I search for to buy a replacement? Tell me which details to check first, like a model number.

Check sizes before ordering. What's the strangest thing in your junk drawer?

If typing on a phone feels slow, tap the microphone in ChatGPT and talk. To make it easy to follow along, start with this:

Keep your answers short and simple, ask me one question at a time, and wait for my answer before moving on.

ChatGPT can also read any answer out loud: press and hold it and choose Read aloud. Do you prefer typing or talking to your phone?

For a letter full of official wording, take a photo with the account numbers covered, add it in ChatGPT with the plus button, and ask:

What is this letter asking me to do, by what date, and what happens if I do nothing? Explain it in plain English.

Call the number printed on the letter if anything is unclear. That's prompt 49 in my $7 shortcuts pack, linked in my profile.

A thank-you note feels personal when it mentions one specific thing. Give the AI that detail:

Write a thank-you note to [person] for [gift or favor]. Mention [one specific detail], keep it to 4 sentences, warm and a little playful.

Then copy it in your own handwriting. Prompt 9, Thank-you note that isn't generic, is in my $7 shortcuts pack in my profile.

A complaint gets a faster answer when it asks for one clear thing by a clear date. Try this:

Write a calm complaint to [company] about [problem]. Include the order number, dates, what I've already tried, and exactly what I'm asking for by [date].

Keep a copy of what you send. Prompt 45, Write a complaint, is in my $7 shortcuts pack, linked in my profile.

Before you call about the phone or internet bill, ask for the script plus a plan for pushback:

Write a short, friendly script for asking [company] for a lower rate. I've been a customer for [time] and pay [amount]. Add 2 polite replies for if they say no.

Have it on screen during the call. Prompt 46, Negotiate a bill, is in my $7 shortcuts pack in my profile.

Before paying a medical bill, line it up with the insurance letter that explains the claim. Upload both with your ID numbers covered and ask:

Do these match? Tell me what I actually owe and anything that looks billed twice. Then write 3 questions for the billing office.

Call with those questions in front of you. My free guide has 10 shortcuts like this, linked in my profile.

Take a photo of the inside of your fridge and upload it with this:

Suggest 3 dinners that use whatever here will spoil soonest. Assume I have basic pantry staples, and keep each one under 30 minutes.

Asking for what spoils first is what keeps food out of the bin. Shortcut 10 in my free guide is the full version, linked in my profile.

Before filling in a long form for school or benefits, upload a blank copy and ask:

Which parts of this form apply to someone in [my situation]? List the documents and numbers I'll need before I start, and explain any confusing questions in plain English.

Gather everything first and it takes one sitting. Keep your real ID numbers out of the chat. My free guide has 10 more shortcuts, linked in my profile.

Helping a parent move or clearing out a family home feels endless until it's in order. Talk or type everything that needs doing, then ask:

Turn this into a step-by-step plan, starting 8 weeks before [moving date]. Group it by week and flag anything that needs a phone call or a booking: [list]

Print it and tick things off. Shortcut 6 in my free guide, Brain dump to plan, is linked in my profile.

Appointments go by fast. Before the next one, give the AI your notes and ask:

Here's what I want to discuss with my [doctor]: [symptoms, dates, medications]. Organize it into a one-page summary and write the 5 questions I should ask.

Bring it on your phone so nothing gets forgotten. Prompt 35, Prepare for a conversation, works for any appointment, and it's in my $7 shortcuts pack in my profile.

To finally learn the smart TV, the new phone or a spreadsheet, ask the AI to slow down to your pace:

Teach me how to [task] on my [device] as a complete beginner. Give me one step at a time and wait until I type next before showing the next step.

That keeps the screen calm. Prompt 31, Explain it like a tutor, is in my $7 shortcuts pack in my profile.

Comparing two options gets easier when the AI knows what matters most to you:

Ask me what matters in choosing [a phone plan] and have me rank it. Then score [option A] and [option B] using my ranking in a table, and tell me what to double-check.

Confirm prices on the company's own site. Prompt 33, Compare options, is in my $7 shortcuts pack, linked in my profile.

topic: A trip with rest built in
text:
Ask for a trip plan that matches the pace you actually like:

Plan [number] days in [place] for [who's going]. Keep it to 2 activities a day, add rest breaks, note where there's seating and how much walking each part involves.

Check opening hours before you go. Prompt 47, Plan a trip, is in my $7 shortcuts pack, linked in my profile.

To save a handwritten recipe card, open ChatGPT, tap the plus button, take a photo of the card and ask:

Type out this recipe exactly as written. Then make a clean version with numbered steps, and mark any word you couldn't read.

Print copies for the family and keep the original safe. Whose handwriting would you most like to save?

When the washer flashes an error code, take a photo of the display and the model sticker and upload both with this:

What does this error mean on this model? List what I can safely check myself, in order, and tell me which signs mean I should call a repair person.

Check anything electrical against the manual. Which appliance in your house has the most mysterious beeps?

A contractor quote is easier to judge once you know what usually goes in one. Paste it in with this:

Here's a quote for [job] in [area]: [paste]. What's normally included in a job like this that's missing here? Write 5 questions I should ask before signing.

Take out names and addresses first. What's the biggest job you've hired someone for?

Before a big purchase, ask the AI to argue against it. It's good at spotting the part you've been skipping past:

I'm about to buy [item] for [price] because [reasons]. Argue against it like a skeptical friend who knows my situation, then tell me what would change your mind.

If its case is weak, buy it happily. What's the last thing you almost bought?

topic: A second opinion on a strange text
text:
When a text says your package is held or your account is locked, take a screenshot before tapping anything, add it in ChatGPT and ask:

What signs in this message are common in scams, and how would the real company usually contact me about this?

Treat it as a second opinion, then contact the company using the number on your card or its official website. Have you had one of these lately?

Most AI apps let you choose whether your chats help train future versions. In ChatGPT it's under Settings, then Data controls, called Improve the model for everyone. In Claude it's under Settings, then Privacy.

Switch it off if you'd like your chats kept out of training, and keep account numbers and passwords out of every chat either way. Did you know this setting existed?

AI can sound completely sure and still get things wrong. After any answer that matters, send this:

Which parts of your answer are you least sure about? Tell me what I should double-check with an official source, and where to look.

It's a good habit for anything about money, health or the law. What would you always double-check?

If you keep retyping the same details, like your budget or who you cook for, save them in the AI's settings once. ChatGPT calls it custom instructions and Claude calls it personal preferences. Write something like:

I live in [place], cook for [people], avoid [foods], and like short answers with steps.

Every new chat starts with it. What detail do you find yourself repeating most?
